alt: Two overlapping circles: deviance breaks social norms and crime breaks the criminal law. Rudeness is deviant but not criminal; minor speeding in many places is criminal but not seen as deviant.
caption: Not all deviance is crime, and not all crime is seen as deviant.

alt: Three arguments: Becker’s labelling and moral entrepreneurs; Cohen’s and Hall’s moral panics; and the Marxist view that law reflects ruling-class interests. Durkheim adds that deviance is normal and functional.
caption: Labels, panics and power all shape what counts as crime.

after: ## Types of crime: what makes each sociologically interesting
alt: Cards for violent and property, white-collar, corporate, state, green, “victimless” and cyber crime, each with what makes it sociologically interesting, and a reminder separating white-collar from corporate crime.
caption: Crimes of the powerful are less visible than violent and property crime.

after: ## Types of crime: what makes each sociologically interesting
alt: Three types of denial from Cohen’s States of Denial: literal denial that it happened, interpretive denial that it was something else, and implicatory denial that accepts the facts but denies their moral implications.
caption: State crime is hidden by literal, interpretive and implicatory denial.

alt: A funnel narrowing from an act taking place, through being noticed, recognised as a crime, reported and recorded, to arrest, charge and conviction. Crime drops out at each stage, creating the dark figure.
caption: Recorded crime is only the narrow end of the funnel.

alt: Official statistics, victim surveys and self-report studies compared by what each is best used for and its main problem.
caption: Each source catches a different part of the dark figure.

after: ## Explaining patterns of offending and victimisation
alt: A grid of offending and victimisation patterns by gender, social class, age and ethnicity, each with explanations such as Pollak’s chivalry thesis, Messerschmidt, Box, Lea and Young, and Hall.
caption: Every pattern needs an explanation, and every explanation has a rival.

alt: A five-step plan for a 20-mark essay on social harm: definitions, arguments for (Box, Bhopal, state crime, zemiology), arguments against (left realists, measurement), application to a named society, and a judgement.
caption: Define, argue both sides, apply to a society, then judge.
